title: Which of these seven questions need data?
description: Seven question cards from the book are sorted into two bins by asking whether the answers vary and must be collected. Keeko doubts that the brick question is statistical just because it says approximately.
teaching_notes: One idea: a statistical question has many answers that vary, so we answer it by collecting data. Watch for students who call a question statistical because it has a number or the word approximately in it.

source: Which of these are statistical questions? (a) the price of a
video_script.why: The child can read a question but has not asked whether its answer comes from one fact or from many values that vary.
video_script.substitution: A statistical question has answers that vary, so the data must be collected.
video_script.anchor: Seven question cards from the book and two bins, one for statistical questions and one for the rest
video_script.wrong_move: judges a question by the word approximately instead of asking whether the answers vary
video_script.payoff_line: Five of the seven questions are statistical questions

final_answer.value: (a), (b), (c), (f) and (g) are statistical questions; (d) and (e) are not
final_answer.spoken: the tennis ball price, the dogs' ages, the hill walking, the best bowler and the Barmer rainfall are statistical questions; the reading question and the bricks are not

maths_rules: seven questions (a) to (g) are the book's
a statistical question can be answered by collecting data whose values vary
(d) has one answer for one person and (e) has one count to estimate, so they are not
5 statistical questions and 2 that are not make 7 in all
video_script.design: Seven cards sit above two bins. Each card is tested by asking whether the answers vary, and then drops into a bin. Only the book's questions are used.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>These are seven questions from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Some ask about prices, some about ages, and some about rainfall.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>One asks whether you like reading.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Which of these questions can be answered only by collecting data?

narration: <bookmark mark='g1'/>A question that can be answered by collecting data is called a statistical question.
<bookmark mark='g2'/>Its answers usually differ from one person or thing to another.

beats.on_screen: Given: (a) price of a tennis ball in India (b) ages of the dogs on this street (c) fraction of your class who like walking up a hill (d) Do you like reading? (e) about how many bricks are in this wall (f) best bowler in yesterday's match (g) rainfall pattern in Barmer last year

marks.given: the seven questions are listed on the board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, seven questions from the book.
One asks the price of a tennis ball in India.
<bookmark mark='g3'/>One asks the ages of the dogs on this street.
One asks what fraction of your class likes walking up a hill.
<bookmark mark='g5'/>One asks, do you like reading?
One asks about how many bricks are in this wall.
<bookmark mark='g7'/>One asks who was the best bowler yesterday.
One asks about the rainfall pattern in Barmer last year.

beats.on_screen: To find: which questions are statistical questions

marks.find: the words statistical questions are underlined

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which of them are statistical questions.

beats.on_screen: Step 1, test: will the answers vary? (a) prices differ between shops and brands; (b) the dogs have different ages; (c) each student says yes or no, and the replies vary. These three: statistical

marks.s1: the tennis ball card shows tags with different prices
marks.s2: the dog card shows tags with different ages
marks.s3: the hill card shows a mix of yes and no tags, and the three cards drop into the left bin

narration: <bookmark mark='s1'/>Step one, ask whether the answers will vary, because then we must collect data.
Prices of a tennis ball differ between shops and brands.
<bookmark mark='s2'/>The dogs have different ages.
<bookmark mark='s3'/>Each student says yes or no about the hill, and the replies vary.
These three are statistical questions.

beats.on_screen: Step 2, test: will the answers vary? (d) one person gives one answer; (e) one wall has one count to estimate. These two: not statistical

marks.d1: the reading card shows a single tag
marks.d2: the brick card shows one wall with a single count

narration: <bookmark mark='d1'/>Step two, apply the same test to the next two.
Do you like reading asks one person, and gives one answer.
<bookmark mark='d2'/>The brick question has one wall and one count to estimate.
Nothing varies, so these two are not statistical questions.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, test: will the answers vary? (f) wickets and runs of several bowlers are data; (g) rainfall changes from day to day and month to month. These two: statistical

marks.c1: the bowler card shows several bowlers with their wickets and runs
marks.c2: the rainfall card shows bars of different heights, and both cards drop into the left bin

narration: <bookmark mark='c1'/>Step three, the last two.
To name the best bowler, we compare the wickets and runs of several bowlers, and those are data.
<bookmark mark='c2'/>The rainfall in Barmer changes from day to day and month to month.
Both are statistical questions.

beats.on_screen: Answer: (a), (b), (c), (f) and (g) are statistical questions; (d) and (e) are not

marks.ans2: the five statistical cards glow in the left bin

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Five of the seven questions are statistical questions.
<bookmark mark='ans2'/>They are the tennis ball price, the dogs' ages and the hill walking.
The other two are the best bowler and the Barmer rainfall.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the board
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's thought bubble holds the brick card with the word approximately circled; the card hovers over the left bin; then the wall shows as one wall and the bubble is struck through

marks.doubt: the bubble with the brick card appears and the word approximately is circled
marks.fix: the wall shows as one wall with one count of bricks

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the brick question is statistical, because it says approximately.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But there is only one wall, and it has one number of bricks.
<bookmark mark='idea'/>We are estimating one count, and nothing varies, so it is not statistical.
